profile.name: Suscia
profile.tagline: A frenetic, sensual circle dance of Afro-Brazilian resistance from Tocantins.
profile.insight: In Tocantins, Brazil, dancers perform the Suscia during the monthlong Festa do Divino Espírito Santo, jumping into the ring to act out being bitten by swarms of stinging jiquitaia ants.
profile.profile: Suscia is a lively Afro-Brazilian folk dance originating from the state of Tocantins, particularly in cities such as Peixe, Natividade, and Arrais. Performed primarily during religious celebrations like the monthlong Festa do Divino Espírito Santo, the dance features a pair hopping in close proximity inside a surrounding circle of singers and drummers. Participants take turns replacing the central dancers via a tap-in system, maintaining a high-energy rhythm. Accompanying instruments are strictly acoustic, including hand-carved, cowhide-topped wooden drums and occasional acoustic guitars.
profile.profile_long:
Suscia (also known variously as Sussa, Suça, Súcia, or Sussia) is an Afro-Brazilian dance tradition deeply rooted in the history of Tocantins in central Brazil. Predominant in towns such as Peixe, Natividade, and Arrais, the dance's origins carry multiple community narratives. Some local accounts attribute its creation to enslaved African labourers brought to the region by gold miners, who were permitted to dance after long workdays. Other traditions hold that the dance was born within quilombos—settlements formed by escaped slaves as acts of resistance against slavery. Regardless of the exact site of origin, the practice carries profound African heritage and forms a vital piece of local cultural memory.

Despite its sensual and energetic choreography, Suscia is fundamentally tied to religious festivities in Tocantins, most notably the monthlong Festa do Divino Espírito Santo. During these traditional feasts, community members assemble in open-air spaces. A central couple—one male and one female—hops in circles in very close proximity to each other. Surrounding them, the community forms a large outer loop, clapping in rhythm, singing short ditties, and beating homemade drums. The church accepts and even encourages the practice during these sacred events, embracing its role in municipal identity.

Technically, the performance relies on continuous circular spatial movement and an interactive tap-in rotation system. Dancers outside the main circle monitor the pair in the center; a man from the outer loop taps the male dancer on the shoulder to take his spot, while a woman subsequently taps the female dancer to take hers. The movement dynamic involves energetic hopping and dramatic pantomime, as demonstrated in popular ditties like 'Formiga que doi e jiquitaia' ('When an ant bite, it is jiquitaia'). Dancers mimic scratching thousands of crawling ants off their bodies—a practice said to stem from an spontaneous incident where dancers stepped onto an ant mound mid-performance.

The soundscape of Suscia is entirely acoustic and relies on handcrafted instrumentation. Community members construct traditional drums by felling trees, burning out the centers to hollow the trunks, and stretching cowhide across one open end. These drums provide the driving beat alongside handclaps, call-and-response vocals, and occasional acoustic string guitars. Songs are brief, often consisting of only a few repetitive verses centered on lighthearted flirting or local humor.

Today, Suscia faces generational shifts as its tradition declines among younger demographics. To preserve this Afro-Brazilian cultural heritage alongside more widely known regional styles, the state government of Tocantins organizes annual Suscia dance competitions aimed at engaging youth in Peixe, Natividade, Arrais, and surrounding municipalities.

sections.origins_and_history: Suscia originated among Afro-Brazilian communities in Tocantins, with debates surrounding whether it was created by enslaved people working for gold miners or within quilombos—settlements established by escaped slaves. The exact historic origin remains contested, and the name varies across communities as Sussa, Suça, Súcia, or Sussia.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a large circle. One male and one female dancer step into the center, hopping in circles in close proximity to one another. Members of the outer circle clap, sing short ditties, and beat drums. Outside participants rotate into the center by tapping the active dancers—men replacing the male dancer and women replacing the female dancer. In specific songs like 'Formiga que doi e jiquitaia', dancers scratch their bodies as part of the pantomime.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for Suscia relies strictly on non-electric, acoustic instrumentation. The musical accompaniment consists of vocals, clapping, and homemade wooden drums created by hollowed-out tree trunks covered with cowhide on one end. Acoustic string guitars are occasionally played to accompany the drumming.
sections.costume_and_setting: Suscia is performed outdoors or in public community gatherings, predominantly in the Tocantins cities of Peixe, Natividade, and Arrais during local religious festivals. Specific traditional costumes are not detailed in the sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is primarily performed during religious celebrations, particularly the monthlong festival of the Festa do Divino Espírito Santo. Despite its sensual nature and songs centered on flirting, the local church supports and encourages the tradition as an integral piece of regional culture.
sections.regional_variants: Variants exist across different municipalities in Tocantins, such as Peixe, Natividade, and Arrais, primarily reflected in minor linguistic variations of the dance's name (Sussa, Suça, Súcia, Sussia).
sections.lineage: Rooted in 18th and 19th-century Afro-Brazilian slave culture and quilombo resistance traditions in central Brazil, Suscia continues today under civic preservation programs sponsored by the state government of Tocantins.

basic_steps: Form a wide outer circle with all participants except one active central couple.
The central male and female couple hop continuously in close proximity in a circular path.
Perform bodily pantomime (e.g., body scratching) matched to the song's verse narrative.
An outer circle member approaches, taps the active dancer of the same gender, and takes their place in the center.
teaching.rhythm: Frenetic drum-driven acoustic rhythm backed by handclaps.
teaching.formation: Outer circle (loop) of singers/clappers surrounding a central male-female pair.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners learn the outer circle clapping and chorus response before taking turns in the central pair via the tap-in rotation.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Frenetic drum beats paired with synchronized handclapping
instruments: Hollowed tree trunk drum with cowhide head
music_profile.vocal_style: Short sung ditties, call-and-response group vocals
music_profile.musical_form: Short repeated verses, often single-verse ditties
music_profile.sound_description: A high-energy acoustic texture driven by deep, handmade cowhide trunk drums and steady handclaps. Call-and-response vocals sing short, playful ditties about flirting and local humor, punctuated by acoustic guitar strumming.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, energetic, ready to hop and move fluidly in close proximity.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Used for expressive pantomime, such as scratching the body during ant-themed songs, and handclapping in the outer circle.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Sensual and dynamic movement centered within a close-partnering ring.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Large outer standing ring enclosing a tight central space where one couple dances.
movement_profile.partnering: One male and one female dancer in close proximity; continuous partner swapping via shoulder tap-ins.

signature_moves.name: Jiquitaia Scratch
signature_moves.description: Dancers scratch their arms and body in rhythm to mimic being bitten by swarms of jiquitaia ants.

signature_moves.name: Tap-In Swap
signature_moves.description: An outer circle dancer taps an inner dancer on the shoulder to instantly replace them in the circle.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Frequent small hops and light jumps while circling.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Do not remain in the center indefinitely; honor the tag-in turn-taking system from the outer ring.

learning_units.description: Outer circle rhythmic clapping and vocal response drill.

Tap-in shoulder rotation mechanics into the center ring.

social_formats.description: Large outer circle of singers/clappers surrounding a central male-female dancing pair.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Ant Farm Dance of Tocantins
episode_brief.logline: In the heart of Brazil, an Afro-Brazilian tradition survives through sacred festivals, frenetic drum rhythms, and playful ant-scratching pantomime.
beats: Opening on the banks of the Tocantins River during the Festa do Divino Espírito Santo.
Crafting a traditional drum from a hollowed tree trunk and cowhide skin.
The outer ring forms: elders clap and sing short ditties as the drum beat accelerates.
A couple enters the center, hopping in close proximity as the crowd cheers.
The 'Jiquitaia' verse begins: dancers pantomime scratching ant bites without losing the rhythm.
Dancers from the outer ring tap in, swapping partners seamlessly.

drills: Practice rhythmic handclapping to acoustic drum beats.
Learn the call-and-response vocal refrain for 'Formiga que doi e jiquitaia'.
Execute continuous light hopping while moving in a circular path with a partner.
Maintain close proximity while navigating spatial awareness.
Integrate upper-body scratching gestures into footwork hopping.
Execute fluid tap-in transitions from the outer loop into the dance center.

visual_motifs: Carved cowhide drums resting on red earth.
Clapping hands forming a wide supportive circle.
Dancers' feet hopping rapidly in tight central circles.
Expressive scratching gestures during playful songs.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An energetic regional culture bearer from Tocantins who emphasizes joy, community connection, and rhythmic precision.
episode_brief.music_cue: A fast, driving acoustic drum beat with clear handclaps and a energetic vocal refrain.

seniors.seated_version: Participants sit in a circle, performing the rhythmic handclapping, singing chorus lines, and executing upper-body ant-scratching gestures in time with the drums.
seniors.standing_version: Perform gentle stationary stepping or slow weight shifts in place while participating in the tap-in outer ring.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduce the tempo to a moderate beat; limit footwork height to low steps rather than high hops.

children.game_version: The 'Jiquitaia Ant Tag' game: children form a ring, and when the lead singer calls out 'jiquitaia!', the central pair must freeze and scratch before tapping the next classmate to jump in.

claims.text: Suscia is a folk dance from the state of Tocantins in Brazil, predominant in cities like Peixe, Natividade and Arrais.
claims.quote: Suscia (or Sussa, Suça, Súcia, Sussia) is a folk dance from the state of Tocantins in Brazil. It is most predominant in cities like Peixe, Natividade and Arrais.

claims.text: Some locals state that Suscia was created by African slaves brought by gold miners, while others trace it to quilombos.
claims.quote: Some locals say that the Suscia was created by African slaves brought to the area by gold miners. After the workday was over, the slave owners would allow their subjects to dance. Others believe that the dance originated in the Quilombo itself.

claims.text: Suscia is predominantly danced during the monthlong festival of Festa do Divino Espírito Santo.
claims.quote: Suscia is mostly danced during religious celebration in the region, especially the Festa do Divino Espírito Santo, which is a monthlong festival.

claims.text: The dance involves one male and one female hopping in circles in close proximity while others form a circle singing and clapping.
claims.quote: Suscia is a frenetic sensual dance, where one male and one female hops in circles in very close proximity of each other. Others stand around in a big loop singing a ditty and clapping to the sound of drums.

claims.text: Central dancers are replaced when outer circle participants tap them and take their spot.
claims.quote: A man from the outside circle taps the male dancer and takes his spot in the center then a woman from the loop taps the female dancer and takes her spot next.

claims.text: Instruments used are strictly non-electric, featuring hollowed tree trunk drums with cowhide heads and occasional guitars.
claims.quote: No electric instruments are used, only vocal, drums and the occasional string guitar. The people from the area usually build their own drums, made by chopping down a tree, making it hollow by burning the wood and attaching a cowhide to one of the ends.

claims.text: The popular ditty 'Formiga que doi e jiquitaia' features dancers scratching their bodies as if crawling with ants.
claims.quote: For example, the most popular one is a ditty with only one verse called “Formiga que doi e jiquitaia”, which translates to “When an ant bite, it is jiquitaia”. This song is danced by the dancers scratching their bodies as if they have thousands of ants crawling over them.

claims.text: The government of Tocantins sponsors annual Suscia dance contests to involve younger generations as the tradition declines.
claims.quote: In order to try to keep this dance alive in the country of samba, the government of the state of Tocantins has been sponsoring Suscia dance contests yearly to get the younger generation involved.

claims.text: Suscia is a subclass of Brazilian folk dance.
